texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp8:
SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.
Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.
If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
“The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”
The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.
This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues.
For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.
The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun.
The FCC did not grant this waiver request “because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements.” The company will need to obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites that are not intended to be disposed of via atmospheric reentry.
However, in other ways the FCC appears to have been incredibly lenient with SpaceX. This is particularly the case with environmental concerns raised by numerous parties that commented on SpaceX’s application to the FCC.
Half a dozen organizations, such as the Secure World Foundation and American Astronomical Society, raised concerns about deploying so many satellites into orbit, citing collision risks, orbital debris, atmospheric pollution from so many satellite reentries, impacts on astronomical observations, and more. The FCC also received approximately 1,500 public comments concerning SpaceX’s application.
Some of these environmental issues, the FCC said, lay beyond the scope of its review. For example, on concerns about the environmental implications of thousands or potentially tens of thousands of rocket launches, the FCC said, “Potential concerns related to the emissions of rocket launches and the subsequent impacts on the human environment as an indirect result of the Starmind system are outside of the Commission’s purview.”
The FCC also rejected calls for further environmental scrutiny of pollution from satellite reentries, including concerns about aluminum oxides and their potential effects on the ozone layer. “Other concerns, including impacts on the atmosphere caused by satellites burning up on re-entry, remain speculative and not supported in the record,” the FCC authorization states.
As part of its decision, the FCC cited a significant policy change adopted in October, when the agency concluded that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC reasoned that as these activities occur beyond US territory, they don’t constitute federal actions requiring environmental review. As a result, the agency declined to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of SpaceX’s Starmind constellation.

The US Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX's plan to deploy up to one million satellites to build data centers in orbit, giving Elon Musk's company a major foothold in the industry. The authorization runs through 2040, as tech firms race to move computing infrastructure into space despite significant technical hurdles.
The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to launch up to one million satellites as part of its plan to build data centers in space. Projects for orbiting data centers have multiplied since last year.
Alongside SpaceX and its Starmind constellation, Google is pursuing its own work under the codename Suncatcher, while Blue Origin has submitted an application to the FCC for its "Project Sunrise."
Several startups are also in the race, including Starcloud, which successfully operated an advanced processor known as a GPU aboard a satellite in late 2025. Google also achieved this in October.
SpaceX's authorization runs until 2040, according to a document published Wednesday on the FCC's website.
SpaceX has the advantage of having its own rockets, which have already completed hundreds of missions.
In August, SpaceX boss Elon Musk promised a first launch into orbit in the fourth quarter of 2027 and a ramp-up in 2028.
The company has struck a deal with Nvidia , which will supply its latest-generation Vera Rubin processors, specially designed to operate in space.
Most space-based data center projects have a similar architecture: a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO), positioned close together to ensure reliable connections between them.
Starmind's satellites will communicate with those already in orbit as part of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet network, which will then relay the data to Earth.
Other competing networks plan to receive data directly from Earth and send it back using lasers.
Not all the technical challenges have been resolved, including processors' ability to withstand the high levels of radiation in space.
Observers also point to the difficulty of withstanding extreme temperatures or avoiding damage from space debris and micrometeorites.
Locating a data center in space offers numerous advantages over building one on Earth.
Among those, a satellite in what is known as a sun-synchronous orbit can capture solar energy continuously and with eight times the efficiency of its ground-based equivalent.

Army hails Iowa’s lead azide detonation, claiming no traces of airborne lead have been detected so far.
United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.
Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.
The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.
“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.
Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.
However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”.
In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.”
Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles.
Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone.
A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.
Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater.
Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead.
Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments.
“The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents.
The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation.
“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg7:
Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.
Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.
On Wednesday evening, the Army said that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.
President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".
"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.
Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.
"Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete," the Army added.
Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin also said on social media that in the hours after the detonation "all EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead".
The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.
He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.
"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.
Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.
The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.
"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.
"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."
Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.
"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.
Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said on X that his state was "seeing little to no impact" from the blast. In a press release, he said he was directing state agencies to remain on standby for any "unanticipated impact".
The Iowa site is only 10 miles (16 km) from the Illinois border.
Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".
Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".
Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.
In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.
It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.
The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.
But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.
Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”
The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”
Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”
In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.
1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.
In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.
It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.
1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.
The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.
Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.
The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.
For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.
The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.
The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.
Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.
Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X , and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened.
The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue .

Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.
Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press .
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here .
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.
Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

A court ruled in favor of the US CPSC’s argument that Amazon is responsible for recalled products that other companies sell on its platforms.
Amazon is on the hook to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after losing its legal battle against the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The US District Court for the District of Maryland ruled in favor of the CPSC, which argued that Amazon is a distributor of goods , not a logistics provider, making it responsible for carrying out recalls of third-party products.
Amazon sued the CPSC in March 2025 after the agency ordered Amazon to recall over 400,000 “Fulfilled by Amazon” products that pose a “substantial product hazard,” including faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers without electrocution protection, and children’s sleepwear that doesn’t meet federal flammability standards.
As a result, Amazon will be required to implement the following measures, initially outlined in the CPSC’s January 2025 order :
On the day CPSC publishes the recall releases, Amazon must notify the public by posting the recall releases to Amazon.com; notify original purchasers directly via email and by providing information regarding the recalls on each purchaser’s “Your Orders” page.
Amazon must provide one round of notice of the recalls to Fulfilled by Amazon participants that sold the subject products.
Amazon must issue a full refund in the amount of the purchase price to any consumer who submits proof of destruction or disposal of a subject product.
Amazon must maintain the recall releases on the “Recalls and Product Safety Alerts” webpage on amazon.com for a minimum of five years.
Amazon must submit monthly progress reports for five years and maintain records of its actions to comply with the Order for the same period.
“We have a longstanding commitment to removing unsafe and recalled products from our store and notifying customers, backed by an industry-leading recalls process,” Amazon spokesperson Sammy Brill says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “We’re reviewing our options following the ruling and look forward to continuing to work with the CPSC to put customer safety first.”

“DART made a really, really large mess. However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess.”
Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.
Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.
But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.
“We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida . On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos . The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.
Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.
“I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” said Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. Therefore, we are in a sort of a transition between just cratering and global transformation, and we are still not sure how this can happen.”
Hera found Didymos, the larger of the two asteroids, spinning on its axis just as DART observed on final approach in 2022. Dimorphos is no longer so stable.
“As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit,” says Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist.
The Hera spacecraft will fly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos over the next six months to obtain more detailed observations. Hera will release two small sub-satellites to attempt landings on Dimorphos and collect data on the asteroid’s composition, internal structure, and mass.
Scientists will use this information to reconstruct the dynamics of DART’s impact four years ago and better understand how a future deflection mission might move an asteroid off a trajectory that actually threatens Earth. Near-Earth asteroids come in many shapes and sizes, with different densities and makeups, so knowledge of Dimorphos’s physical properties will anchor predictive computer models teaching scientists how best to deflect all types of asteroids.
“Once we understand, we have a breakthrough, which really solves planetary defense,” Michel said in an interview with Ars.
In its initial reconnaissance this month, Hera spotted hundreds of boulders surrounding the double asteroid. This was not entirely unexpected. A picture taken by the Hubble Space Telescope shortly after DART’s impact showed a cloud of material streaming behind Didymos and Dimorphos , but scientists were astonished by the extent of the debris swarm in Hera’s first images.
“As we approached Didymos and Dimorphos, we quickly realized the asteroids were not alone,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. “In fact, they had a lot of company.”
An image released by ESA on Wednesday combines 11 long exposure frames from Hera’s hyperspectral camera. Image processors on the ground digitally removed the relatively bright Didymos and Dimorphos to reveal a panoply of dimmer streaks and dots, each of which is a rock fragment ranging in size from a football to a washing machine, Murdoch said.
“Hera came to visit two asteroids, and we found hundreds of companions,” Murdoch said.
One obvious explanation for the boulders is they were thrown off Dimorphos when DART slammed into it. But scientists cautioned they need more information before they can say that with surety. Hera is the first space mission to undertake a sustained study of an asteroid with its own moon. The debris around the two asteroids might be relics from the creation of Dimorphos some time in the ancient past.
“Hera will allow us to study that in more detail,” Murdoch said. “We really need to know more about these boulders and characterize them to understand if they’re linked to DART, if they’re linked to another process, and what the consequences might be for other asteroid systems in the Solar System.”
The boulder field will create challenges for navigating around the asteroids. In particular, the boulders are an added risk for the two small CubeSats Hera is supposed to deploy in January.
“We saw a couple of images that didn’t reassure me,” said Margherita Cardi, project manager for the Milani CubeSat. “There is a mix of excitement and panic.”
Claudia Balossi, spacecraft systems engineer for Hera’s other CubeSat, named Juventas, said her mission’s planned trajectory would take it right through the boulders as it moves within a couple of miles of the asteroids, then finally toward a landing attempt on Dimorphos, where it will measure the miniature world’s tenuous gravity field.
“We are right in the middle of it,” Balossi said. “The smallest ones are probably just as big as we are and the biggest ones are very big. In the worst case, a boulder will land on us. We will activate our gravimeter right away [if that happens],” Balossi joked.
The good news is the asteroids’ gravity is so weak that Hera, Milani, Juventas, and the hazards around them all move at snail-like speeds. Hera’s current trajectory takes it around the asteroids at a relative velocity of just a quarter-mile per hour, or about 12 centimeters per second. At that speed, there’s no danger of a sudden catastrophic hypervelocity collision between the spacecraft and the boulders lurking nearby.
Scientists have seen this at an asteroid before. NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft kicked up an estimated six tons of rock and dust when it gently moved in to collect a sample from an asteroid named Bennu in 2020. Low gravity and weak surface cohesion are a recipe for outsized effects.
“These types of bodies, because of their low gravity, have a very counterintuitive behavior,” Michel said. “Each time we interact with them, whether to take a sample or to make an impact, the response of the surface was not the one we predicted, simply because our intuition relies on what we experience every day on Earth. Even if the rules of physics are the same in the Universe, they express very differently depending on local attraction.”

That’s what makes travelers so fun to buy for. But you don’t want to get them just anything. The key is to find that clever gift even they didn’t know they needed, and that’s where we come in. From streaming gadgets for the hotel to portable espresso makers and high-capacity chargers , these are our favorite gifts to help travelers take their next adventure to the next level.
Give Yourself A Gift With Holiday Travel Deals . Make the most of the season with limited-time holiday offers on travel and more. However you choose to celebrate, explore more ways to save and make your next journey even more rewarding. Terms apply. Ends December 15, 2026.

Few things are more frustrating on a long flight than trying to keep your phone stable between your seasoned pretzels and fellow passengers. Thankfully, MiiKare’s adjustable, inexpensive clamp can make things less stressful for your favorite frequent flyer, so they can finally watch Olympus Has Fallen in peace.
We all tend to skimp on simple items for ourselves, which is why this fancy-pants sleep mask makes such a thoughtful present. Its 3D contoured fit is designed to block all light while providing plush memory foam comfort so your loved one can get the rest they need between adventures.
For frequent flyers, a plain suitcase sticker may not be enough. In the age of QR codes, Pebblebee’s Link Bag Tags make a lot more sense. They’re battery-free, scannable by anyone with a phone, and offer built-in privacy with the ability to share or deny personal information.
They say once you go bidet, you never go back. That’s certainly harder to achieve when traveling outside Japan, though Tushy offers an effective solution with its handy, collapsible bidet. The manual contraption isn’t heated, but one portable bathroom luxury at a time.
Mechanism’s clever, durable creations are a favorite here at The Verge . Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.
Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.
First spotted by Patentlyze , the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.
According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall . The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.
Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.
My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.
When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.
Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.
Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.
Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.
Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.
According to the company, Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers. Compared to the number of people using Google Search or even Bing or DuckDuckGo, that’s not much. But the pitch is that with Google, the user is the product, not the customer, and that paying anywhere from $5 to $25 per month (there are multiple plans; unlimited search queries is in the $10 per month plan) helps users escape from that devil’s bargain.
Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.
The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)
Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail. The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now. There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.
Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com .
The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.
According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.
Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.
Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.
“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.
The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.
“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”
Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.
“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.
The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.
That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees .
Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.
The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

Forecasters say high winds on Thursday may spoil the annual march of huge balloons and have moved the parade to Saturday
New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed due to excessively windy weather and will now be held on Saturday.
Forecasters say an impending storm on Thursday may spoil the street party, which is marked by a march of huge balloons. AccuWeather is forecasting winds of 12 to 25 mph (19 to 40 km/h) and rain later on Thursday.
Under guidelines, large balloons must stay grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 km/h) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 km/h). The parade balloons have been grounded only once previously, in 1971.
NBC quoted Macy’s as saying: “The safety of our participants and spectators is our priority.”
Macy’s added: “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”
This year the parade will include a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer and Holly Robinson Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus. Nine Broadway shows will be featured as part of a 10-minute medley, replacing the traditional sprinkling of full show numbers.
The Macy’s parade began more than a century ago in 1924 as a way of creating buzz for the giant department store’s holiday windows at Macy’s Herald Square flagship store in Manhattan. Macy’s borrowed animals from the Central Park Zoo for the first parades but in 1927 ended that practice after children were getting scared.
The animals were then replaced with air-filled balloons and, a year later, balloons that could be filled with helium – a now familiar sight for people around the world from countless Hollywood movies set in New York City.
The parades have been fully cancelled previously only in 1942, 1943 and 1944 because the valuable materials needed to create the huge balloons were diverted for the the second world war effort against Germany and Japan.

New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade
Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.
Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.
The last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.
A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.
The balloons will be deflated again and then re-inflated for Saturday
The potent nor'easter storm is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.
Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.
"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.
Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.
Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.
"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."
Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".
Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.
BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.
During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.
The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade was due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern US as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow, BBC Weather reports.
The governor of the neighbouring state of New Jersey on Wednesday declared a state of emergency across the state's 21 counties, beginning at 18:00 local time (23:00 GMT).
Governor Mikie Sherrill's office said the powerful coastal storm is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall, and severe tidal flooding through Friday, with coastal and bayside communities facing the greatest risk. Sherrill urged residents to stay off the roads as much as possible once the storm arrives.
Originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade, the celebration, which also features live performers, debuted in 1924 as a way to boost holiday sales. It was founded by Macy's employees and their families.
From 1942 to 1944 New York went without the parade as the US directed materials like rubber and helium toward the country's war effort.
The 2.5mi (4km) procession route begins at Macy's Herald Square flagship store and concludes in Manhattan's Upper West Side, with performers and spectators lining the streets to greet Santa Claus and ring in the holiday season.
Country artist Megan Moroney and Grammy nominee Teddy Swims were slated to perform at the flagship store, but it is unclear whether they, along with the dozens of celebrities and float performers on the roster, would be returning on Saturday.

The parade, which marks its 100th edition, got a last-minute rain check ahead of heavy gusts on Thursday.
New York City is famous for its annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, a procession of towering helium balloons, elaborate floats and marching bands.
But on Wednesday, organisers in the United States announced that this year’s edition has been postponed because of an East Coast storm that threatens turbulent weather.

The parade, founded in 1924, was cancelled three times during World War II, but this year marks the first time it was postponed.
The event’s signature balloons were already being inflated on Wednesday when Macy’s announced the delay.
The decision came amid warnings issued by the National Weather Service of lashing winds and possible coastal flooding for the New York City area.

Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%
Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.
The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs.
The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations.
Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.
This is the second major batch of section 301 tariffs, after the White House announced a broad slate of tariffs on more than 80 countries in July, including the UK, Mexico and Canada, saying the countries had failed to enforce bans on forced labor. A lawsuit fighting those tariffs is currently awaiting a decision in the court of international trade.
“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said in a statement on Wednesday.
“President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”
Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 annually in costs for each US household.
The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.

A powerful storm forecast to bring fierce winds and heavy rain to the northeastern United States has forced the unprecedented postponement of the city's 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, with the event rescheduled for Saturday. Officials warned that Thursday's conditions could bring down tree limbs and power lines, while posing a safety risk to the parade's giant balloons and the crowds below.
Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will also be a first: Organizers made an unprecedented decision to postpone the event to Saturday because of bad weather .
The annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, has been moved “out of an abundance of caution" and following consultation with city officials about the severe weather, Macy's said in a statement Wednesday.
“Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized,” the company said.
The postponement came as New York City is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised worries about how the parade's massive balloons would fare while floating through the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers and over throngs of spectators lining the streets below.
At a news conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday's winds will be strong enough to snap tree limbs and down power lines, and he stressed that rescheduling the parade was the right call.
“Now, I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," he said. “Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first.”
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday. The city's emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty tractor-trailers from bridges Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether the event’s expansive lineup would also shift to the new date, though representatives for Broadway shows “Chicago” and “Hamilton” said their performers will make the switch to Saturday.
The parade's iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy’s representatives had repeatedly put off interviews on-site, raising eyebrows among the city's news media ahead of the official postponement.
Will Coss, a Macy's executive, said organizers are working with bands and other performers and are “optimistic that we're going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce and to deliver to New York City on Thanksgiving.”
“Everyone understands what we're up against and is rallying behind us to create the best and most successful 100th parade,” he said.
A spokesperson for the retail giant said it was the first time the event has been postponed. It was canceled for three years — in 1942, 1943 and 1944 — during World War II, the spokesperson said.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma. Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.

Musician who had huge 1980s chart success had been diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018
Andy Taylor, the guitarist with 80s pop megastars Duran Duran , has died aged 65.
He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, which he disclosed publicly in 2022 when Duran Duran were about to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” read a statement shared with Variety . “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”
A statement from Duran Duran added: “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”
Taylor was born in 1961 and grew up in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in a family who worked in the local fishing industry. He began playing guitar from the age of 11 and was tutored by Dave Black of the David Bowie backing band the Spiders from Mars. He left school early to start playing in bands on the working men’s club scene.
In 1980 he joined the nascent Duran Duran, who had formed in 1978 but whose lineup was far from settled – they advertised for a guitarist in Melody Maker, and Taylor travelled to Birmingham to audition. “A couple of days later they rang me and said out of 40 or so I was the only one who knew how to tune up, let alone play,” he later recalled.
The following month Simon Le Bon joined as frontman, by February 1981 they had released their debut single Planet Earth, and with the July release of Girls on Film – a song propelled by Taylor’s ultra-tight and rhythmic playing – they became major stars in the UK and US. Rio, their second album released in 1982, cemented their international playboy image and went Top 10 in both countries, and follow-up Seven and the Ragged Tiger topped the UK chart. Speaking to Smash Hits in 1983, Taylor described his new-found career as “a hobby gone mad”. That year Taylor also opened a wine bar called Rio, in Whitley Bay in his native Tyneside.
Following their third album Duran Duran went on a brief hiatus, during which time Taylor and bassist John Taylor (no relation) formed a new funk-rock group, the Power Station, with singer Robert Palmer and former Chic drummer Tony Thompson. Two singles, the original track Some Like It Hot and a cover of T Rex’s Get It On, reached the US Top 10 in 1985.
Later that year Taylor rejoined Duran Duran to record A View to a Kill, the US chart-topping James Bond film theme, and perform with them at Live Aid in Philadelphia. But amid drug use, relations had become strained: drummer Roger Taylor left due to exhaustion, and Andy Taylor himself left to pursue the rockier direction he began with the Power Station – though his Duran Duran bandmates initially believed he would be continuing with the band.
“I’d come close to a nervous breakdown from the stresses of our crazy life and my own cocaine problem,” Taylor later said. “Combine that with all the shouting matches and the icy silences – I just knew I had to get out. So I did. The day after Live Aid, I stopped drinking and taking drugs. And I quietly started getting legal advice on extricating myself from Duran Duran.”
Collaborating with Sex Pistols’ Steve Jones, he released a solo LP, Thunder, in 1986, and the single Take It Easy was a minor US hit. As well as recording a covers album, Dangerous, he spent a number of years as a writer and producer for hire, with his song Lost in You becoming a transatlantic hit for Rod Stewart in 1988.
The Power Station briefly reunited in 1996, and then in 2000, the classic lineup of Duran Duran reformed and released a new album together, Astronaut, in 2004. He also toured with the band and worked on another (later scrapped) album Reportage, but was hit hard by the death of his father to cancer, and left the band again in 2006; he was diagnosed with depression the following year.
He spent the next decade away from music, first publishing his memoir Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran in 2008. He released a new solo single in 2019 and joined British rock band Reef as a tour guitarist, also producing their 2022 album Shoot Me Your Ace.
Despite the at-times fractious relationship with Duran Duran over the years, Taylor said in his statement accompanying the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction that there was no “bad blood … just pure love and respect for everything we wrote, recorded and achieved together”.
He married his wife Tracey Wilson in 1982, and they had four children together: Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.
Following his cancer diagnosis, he credited his successful music career with keeping him upbeat. “I’ve been very fortunate, I’ve had so much, in terms of living the dream, but because I do music, I think that’s probably really helped me to live with pessimism of an incurable disease,” he said.
